mainTopic: שיור in sales and gifts, and the rules of a שכיב מרע's gifts: dividing, reconsidering, partial retraction, holy gifts, and the wording of a gift.
overview: The גמרא first asks whether keeping back an upper story (דיוטא) counts as a שיור. רבא quoting רב נחמן rules that selling a house 'except for the upper story' is a שיור, because the seller also keeps the right to stick out beams (זיזין). In the same way, giving a palm tree 'except for its fruit' keeps the space of the fruit. Next, רב נחמן teaches about a שכיב מרע who gives away all his property. If he divided it in one plan, he can take it all back if he recovers. If he reconsidered between gifts, he can take back only the last one. He also cannot take back a gift of all his known property, since he may own land elsewhere. The גמרא then rules that taking back part of a deathbed gift cancels the whole gift, proving this from a ברייתא. Questions about a dying man's הקדש, הפקר and צדקה end in תיקו. Finally, רב ששת lists the words that make a gift, and a ברייתא adds inheritance words for a fitting heir, following רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא.

steps.title: House to one person, upper story to another: is that a reserving?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether giving the house to one person and the upper story to another counts as a שיור.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: if the house goes to one person and the upper story to another, what is the law? Does that count as keeping something back, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a question (איבעיא להו). It asks whether splitting a building, with the house going to one person and the upper story to another, counts as a שיור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The issue is whether the person who gets the upper story gets only the room itself, or also extra rights tied to it. If he gets extra rights, the split counts as a שיור.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked before them (the חכמים)
Upper story of a house
Keeping something back; not giving away everything
What is the law?

phrases.english: A question was asked before them:
A house to one person and the upper story to another,
phrases.notes: 'House' here means the lower floor, as opposed to the upper story.

phrases.english: what is the law?
Is it considered a keeping-back, or not?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether splitting a house and its upper story between two people counts as a שיור of extra rights.

steps.title: Follow-up question: selling a house except for its upper story
steps.stepSummary: Even if splitting between two people is not a שיור, what happens when the seller keeps the upper story for himself?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say that a house to one and an upper story to another is not a keeping-back, then what about selling a house 'except for the upper story'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a second question that builds on the first. Suppose the first case is not a שיור. What if the owner sells the house and says 'except for the upper story', keeping it for himself?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'if you will say' show that the second question only matters if the first answer is 'no'. A person keeping something for himself may hold back more than a person who is simply given a room.

keyTerms.meaning: If you will say; introduces a follow-up question that assumes one answer to the first
Except for

phrases.english: If you will say
that a house to one and the upper story to another
is not considered a keeping-back,
then 'except for the upper story', what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follow-up question that assumes a 'no' answer to step 1
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a seller who says 'except for the upper story' is keeping extra rights for himself.

steps.title: רב נחמן: 'Except for the upper story' is a reserving
steps.stepSummary: רבא quoting רב נחמן rules that 'except for the upper story' counts as a שיור, following רב זביד.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said in the name of רב נחמן: even if a house to one and an upper story to another is not a keeping-back, 'except for the upper story' is a keeping-back. This follows רב זביד, who said that if the seller wants to stick out beams from the upper story, he may.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא, quoting רב נחמן, answers the second question: saying 'except for the upper story' is a שיור. He bases this on רב זביד, who says the seller may stick out beams (זיזין) from his upper story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the first case is not a שיור, the second one is. A seller who keeps the upper story keeps more than the room itself. According to רב זביד, he also keeps the right to stick beams out into the air space. That extra right is what makes it a שיור.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the opinion of
Beams or ledges sticking out from a wall
To stick out, to extend outward

phrases.english: Rava said that Rav Nachman said:
If you will say
that a house to one and the upper story to another
is not a keeping-back,
'except for the upper story' is a keeping-back,
and this follows Rav Zevid, who said:
that if he wants to stick out beams from it,
phrases.notes: 'It' means the upper story he kept, so the beams would stick out over the sold area below.

phrases.english: he may stick them out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the follow-up question in step 2
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Except for the upper story' is a שיור, because, following רב זביד, the seller also keeps the right to stick out זיזין.

steps.title: Applying the rule: 'except for its fruit' keeps the space of the fruit
steps.stepSummary: Keeping the upper story also keeps the space for beams. In the same way, saying 'except for its fruit' keeps the space where the fruit hangs, so it is a שיור.
steps.simpleTranslation: So we see: since he kept the upper story, he also kept the space for the beams. Here too, since he said 'except for its fruit', he kept the space of the fruit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a conclusion from רב נחמן's answer and applies it to the earlier palm tree case. Someone who gives a tree 'except for its fruit' keeps the space where the fruit grows, so this counts as a שיור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Keeping one thing brings the space it needs along with it. The upper story comes with its beam space, and the fruit comes with its hanging space. That kept space is what makes it a real שיור, and not just keeping some fruit.

keyTerms.meaning: So we see; evidently
Here too; applying the same logic to our case
The space where the fruit hangs
He kept back

steps.whatToRemember: When someone keeps a part (an upper story, or a tree's fruit), he also keeps the space that part needs. That is why 'except for its fruit' counts as a שיור.

phrases.english: So we see: since he kept the upper story,
he also kept the space for the beams;
here too, since he said
'except for its fruit',
phrases.notes: This goes back to the earlier case of giving a palm tree but keeping its fruit.

phrases.english: he kept the space of the fruit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רב נחמן's rule to the earlier palm tree case
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Saying 'except for its fruit' keeps the space of the fruit, so it counts as a שיור.

steps.title: שכיב מרע who divided all his property: dies, they acquire; recovers, he takes it back
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן teaches that we look at how a שכיב מרע wrote his gifts. If he was dividing his property among people, they acquire if he dies, and he can take everything back if he recovers.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף בר מניומי said in the name of רב נחמן: a dying person who wrote all his property to others, we look at the case. If he was dividing it: if he dies, they all acquire; if he recovers, he takes back all of it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins, going back to the משנה about a שכיב מרע who gives away all his property. רב נחמן says we check whether he was dividing his property among several people, and gives the rule for that case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he was dividing his property, the gifts form one plan of giving away everything, with nothing kept back. So the gifts follow the rule for a שכיב מרע: they take effect if he dies, and are cancelled if he recovers. The words 'if he was dividing' set up the contrasting case, which comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who is dangerously ill, on his deathbed
We look and examine the case
Dividing (his property among several people)
He recovered (literally, he stood up)
He takes back; he retracts

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume that dividing the property among several people means each gift stands alone and stays valid. Here, if he recovers, he takes back ALL the gifts.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Rav Yosef bar Minyumi said that Rav Nachman said:
A dying person who wrote
all his property to others,
we examine the case;
if he was dividing it,
if he dies, they all acquire;
if he recovers, he takes back all of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic: back to the משנה's rule about a שכיב מרע giving away all his property
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a שכיב מרע divides all his property among others, they all acquire if he dies, and he can take back all of it if he recovers.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up how to judge a dying person's gifts: we look at whether they were one plan of dividing everything.

steps.title: When the sick man stopped and changed his mind between gifts
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן continues: if the שכיב מרע paused and reconsidered between gifts, all recipients acquire if he dies. If he recovers, he can take back only the last gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it looks like he was changing his mind as he went: if he dies, all of them acquire. If he recovers, he can take back only the last gift.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רב נחמן's teaching from the last step. Now it gives the second case, where the sick man was reconsidering between gifts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he paused and changed his mind, his first gifts were not meant to cover everything, because he was still keeping something for himself. A gift where he keeps some property is a normal gift, so it stays even if he recovers. Only the last gift, which used up everything, is a 'deathbed gift' that he can cancel.

keyTerms.meaning: Reconsidering, changing his mind partway
He recovered (literally 'he stood up')
The last one, here the last gift

phrases.english: If he was reconsidering,
phrases.notes: He means: he gave one gift, stopped to think, and then decided to give away more.

phrases.english: if he dies, they all acquire;
if he recovers, he can take back only the last one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second half of רב נחמן's teaching begun in step 5
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If he reconsidered between gifts, the earlier gifts stand even if he recovers; only the last can be taken back.

steps.title: Maybe he was just thinking about who gets what
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: maybe the pause doesn't show he changed his mind. Maybe he always meant to give everything and was just deciding who gets each part.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe he was just thinking it over and then giving!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the idea that a pause means he changed his mind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the pause was only to plan how to split things, he planned from the start to give everything away. Then all the gifts together would be one deathbed gift, and he could cancel all of them if he recovers.

keyTerms.meaning: But maybe
Considering, thinking it over

phrases.english: But maybe he was just considering,
and then giving!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption in step 6
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that a pause between gifts shows he changed his mind
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A pause could just be planning the split, which would make it all one gift of everything.

steps.title: A sick man plans first and then gives
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that a שכיב מרע normally thinks everything through before he starts giving. So a pause in the middle shows he changed his mind.
steps.simpleTranslation: The usual way of a sick man is to think carefully first, and only then give.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by describing how a dying person usually acts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sick man finishes his planning before he starts handing out gifts. So if he stops in the middle, it was not for planning. It means he only now decided to give more, and the ruling in step 6 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: The usual way, the normal case
He thinks it through carefully

phrases.english: The usual way of a sick man
is to think it through carefully and then give.

steps.triggerLanguage: סְתָמֵיהּ דִּשְׁכִיב מְרַע מִידָּק דָּיֵיק וַהֲדַר יָהֵיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A pause might just be planning.
steps.terutzMaskana: Planning happens before giving, so a pause shows a change of mind.
steps.whatToRemember: Gifts given in one go are one deathbed gift. If he paused and changed his mind, the earlier gifts stand even if he recovers.

steps.title: He gave away everything and recovered, but may own land elsewhere
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that a שכיב מרע who wrote all his property to others and recovered cannot take it back. We worry he may have property in another place.
steps.simpleTranslation: A sick man who wrote all his property to others and then recovered cannot take it back. We worry that maybe he has property in another country.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching from רב נחמן about a sick man who gave away 'everything' and then got better.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a deathbed gift of everything is cancelled when he recovers. But maybe he owns land somewhere else that we don't know about. If so, he kept something for himself, and the gift is a regular gift that cannot be cancelled.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who is dangerously ill
We are concerned, we worry
Another country or province

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Rav Aḥa bar Minyumi said that Rav Naḥman said:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁכִיב מְרַע שֶׁכָּתַב כׇּל נְכָסָיו לַאֲחֵרִים,
phrases.english: A sick man who wrote all his property to others,
and then recovered, cannot take it back,
because we worry that maybe he has
property in another country.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New teaching on a related topic
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sick man who gave away all his known property and recovered cannot take it back, because he may own land elsewhere.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not say a full deathbed gift is never cancelled. It says we can't be sure he really gave away everything.

steps.title: Then when does the משנה's case ever happen?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: the משנה says that if he kept no land at all, the gift is cancelled when he recovers. With רב נחמן's worry, how could that case ever happen?
steps.simpleTranslation: But the משנה teaches: if he did not keep any land at all, his gift does not stand. How can you ever find that case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן from the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we always worry he has land somewhere else, we could never be sure he kept nothing. So the משנה's case, where the gift is cancelled, would seem impossible.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
He kept back, held something for himself
How can you find this case?

phrases.english: But then our משנה, which teaches:
If he did not keep any land at all,
his gift does not stand;
phrases.notes: He means it does not stand once he recovers.

phrases.english: how can you ever find that case?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 9 from the משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's worry about land elsewhere
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If we always worry about other land, the משנה's case of keeping nothing could never happen.

steps.title: רב חמא: he said 'all my property'
steps.stepSummary: רב חמא answers that the משנה means he said 'all my property.' Those words include any land elsewhere too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חמא said: It is when he says 'all my property.'
steps.whatsHappening: The first answer to the challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן was talking about someone who listed his known property. If he says 'all my property,' that covers land in any place, so he surely kept nothing. Then the gift is cancelled when he recovers, as the משנה says.

keyTerms.meaning: All my property

phrases.english: Rav Ḥama said:
It is when he says, 'All my property.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 10
steps.terutzMaskana: When he says 'all my property,' nothing is left, so the gift is cancelled.

steps.title: מר בר רב אשי: we know he has nothing else
steps.stepSummary: מר בר רב אשי gives a different answer: the משנה is a case where we know he owns nothing elsewhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר רב אשי said: It is when we know for sure that he doesn't have any other property.
steps.whatsHappening: A second, different answer to the same challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the answer is about what we know, not his words. If it is clear he owns no other land, there is nothing to worry about, so he kept nothing and the gift is cancelled if he recovers.

keyTerms.meaning: It is known to us, we presume
He does not have

phrases.english: Mar bar Rav Ashi said:
It is when we know that he has no other property.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: בְּמוּחְזָק לַן דְּלֵית לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to step 10, different from step 11
steps.terutzMaskana: When we know he has no other land, the gift is cancelled.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's case happens either when he says 'all my property' (רב חמא) or when we know he owns nothing else (מר בר רב אשי).

steps.title: Does taking back part cancel the whole gift?
steps.stepSummary: A new question: if a שכיב מרע takes back part of his gift, does that cancel the entire gift?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: Is taking back part of a gift the same as taking back all of it, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about a sick man who takes back only some of his gift.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שכיב מרע can change his mind about his gift. The question is whether changing part of it shows he regrets the whole gift, so the first person loses everything.

keyTerms.meaning: They asked, a question was raised
Taking back part of a gift

phrases.english: They asked:
Taking back part of a gift,
is it taking back the whole thing, or not?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New question
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether partly taking back a deathbed gift cancels the whole gift

steps.title: A proof: all to the first, part to the second
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: he gave everything to the first person and then part to the second; the second acquires and the first gets nothing. The גמרא suggests this is when he died, which would show partial taking back cancels everything.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If he gave all of it to the first person and part of it to the second, the second acquires and the first does not. Isn't this talking about when he died?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question with a ברייתא. It ends by asking whether this is a case where he died, setting up the proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he died, he can't be taking the gift back by recovering. The only reason the first person loses even the part not given to the second would be that taking back part cancels the whole gift. That would answer the question.

keyTerms.meaning: What, is it not...? A suggested reading

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If he gave all of them to the first and part of them to the second,
phrases.notes: 'Them' means his properties: first he gave everything to one person, then gave part to someone else.

phrases.english: the second acquires, the first does not acquire.
What, is it not when he died?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: כּוּלָּן לָרִאשׁוֹן וּמִקְצָתָן לַשֵּׁנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question of step 13
steps.raayaObject: That taking back part of a gift cancels the whole gift
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא where the first person gets nothing after part was given to a second person, read as a case where the giver died

steps.title: No proof: the case is where he got better
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof by saying the ברייתא is talking about a case where the giver recovered.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the ברייתא is talking about a case where he recovered.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the proof from step 14. It says the ברייתא is not about a giver who died. It is about one who got better.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he recovered, the first gift falls apart on its own, because he gave away everything and kept nothing. The second gift was only part of his property, so it stands. That explains the ruling without saying that taking back part cancels the whole gift.

keyTerms.meaning: when he got up, meaning he recovered from his illness
a person who is dangerously ill

steps.confusionAlert: There are two separate reasons a gift can fall apart: taking it back, and getting better after giving away everything. This step uses the second reason, not the first.

phrases.english: No, it is where he recovered.
phrases.notes: Recall the rule from the משנה: if he gave away everything and then got better, the gift is cancelled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the 'he died' reading that step 14 used as a proof.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from the ברייתא. It makes no ruling on the question itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be read as a case where he recovered. Then the first gift fails because he kept nothing, not because of any taking back.

steps.title: The second half of the ברייתא supports the 'got better' reading
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's second half only makes sense if he recovered, which supports the rejection.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too it makes sense, because the end of the ברייתא teaches: if he gave part to the first and all to the second, the first acquires and the second does not. If the case is where he recovered, that explains why the second does not acquire. But if it is where he died, both should acquire!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the 'he recovered' reading with proof from the second half of the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the second half, the second person received everything. If the giver got better, that gift is cancelled because he kept nothing, so 'the second does not acquire' fits well. If the giver died, there is no reason for the second gift to fail, so the ruling would make no sense.

keyTerms.meaning: so too it makes sense; this supports the last point
the last part of a teaching
part of them, meaning part of his property
granted, this works well

phrases.english: So too it is reasonable,
since the last part teaches:
part to the first, and all to the second,
the first acquired, the second did not acquire.
Granted, if you say it is where he recovered,
that is why the second did not acquire;
but if you say it is where he died,
both of them should acquire!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rejection in step 15.
steps.raayaObject: The ברייתא is a case where the giver recovered.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The second half of the same ברייתא: part to the first and all to the second, and the second does not acquire.

steps.title: רב יימר: even if he got better, the proof still works
steps.stepSummary: רב יימר shows that even in the 'got better' case, the first half of the ברייתא proves that taking back part cancels the whole gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יימר said to רב אשי: Let it be where he recovered. Granted, if taking back part counts as taking back all, that is why at least the second acquires. But if taking back part does not count as taking back all, he is like someone dividing all his property between them, and neither one should acquire!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יימר brings the proof back to life. He agrees the case is one where the giver recovered, and he shows the proof still holds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first half, he gave everything to the first person and then part to the second. If taking back part cancels the whole first gift, then only the second gift is left, and it is just part of his property, so it stands. If not, the first person still holds the rest, so he gave away everything between the two and kept nothing. Once he recovered, neither gift should stand. Since the ברייתא says the second does acquire, taking back part must cancel the whole gift.

keyTerms.meaning: taking back part of a gift
taking back the whole gift
like someone dividing his property among people
at least

steps.whyThisMatters: This turns a proof that was knocked down into a strong proof, and it leads straight to the final ruling.

granted, if you say

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the 'he recovered' reading from steps 15-16 but shows the proof for step 13's question still works.

steps.raayaSupportSource: The first half of the ברייתא, read as a case where he recovered: the second person acquires.

steps.title: The ruling: taking back part cancels the whole gift
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה is that taking back part counts as taking back all. The first half of the ברייתא can happen whether he died or recovered, but the second half only when he recovered.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הלכה is: taking back part is taking back all. The first half of the ברייתא can happen whether he died or recovered. The second half can only happen where he recovered.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final ruling and explains which situations each half of the ברייתא fits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first half, the second person wins either way. If he died, the later gift cancels the whole first gift. If he recovered, the whole first gift is cancelled by taking back part, as רב יימר showed. In the second half, the second person loses only because he got everything and the giver recovered, so it fits only the 'recovered' case.

keyTerms.meaning: and the practical ruling is
the first part of a teaching
you can find it, meaning this case can happen

steps.whatToRemember: If a שכיב מרע takes back part of his gift, the whole gift is cancelled. The first half of the ברייתא works whether he died or recovered. The second half works only if he recovered.

phrases.english: And the halacha is:
taking back part is taking back all;
the first part, you find it
whether he died or he recovered,
the last part, you do not find it
except where he recovered.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהִלְכְתָא: חֲזָרָה בְּמִקְצָת הָוְיָא חֲזָרָה בְּכוּלָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts רב יימר's proof as the ruling and matches each half of the ברייתא to its cases.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Taking back part of a gift cancels the whole gift. The ברייתא's first half applies whether he died or recovered; its second half applies only where he recovered.

steps.title: A dying man gave all his property to הקדש and then recovered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if a שכיב מרע gave all his property to הקדש and then got better, does the הקדש stand? Maybe for הקדש he fully commits. Or maybe, since this is about his own life, he does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: if he made all his property holy and then got better, what is the law? Do we say that when it comes to הקדש, a person fully decides to give it over? Or maybe, when it is about himself, he does not fully decide to give it over?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. Does the usual rule, that a dying man's gift is cancelled if he recovers, also apply to a gift to הקדש?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A regular deathbed gift is cancelled on recovery because he only gave it thinking he would die. The question is whether giving to הקדש is different: maybe a person gives to the Temple wholeheartedly no matter what. The other side says that since the whole matter depends on his own survival, he never meant to give it all away if he lived.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among the חכמים (opens a question with no known answer)
He made it holy, giving it to the Temple treasury (הקדש)
And he got up, meaning he recovered from his illness
He fully decides and transfers ownership
Anything that concerns himself, his own life and survival

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not whether הקדש works at all. It clearly works if he dies. The question is only whether it stays in place once he recovers.

phrases.english: They asked:
If he made all his property holy and then recovered, what is the law?
phrases.notes: 'He' is a person on his deathbed, like in the case the גמרא has been discussing.

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן: כֹּל לְגַבֵּי הֶקְדֵּשׁ – גָּמַר וּמַקְנֵי;
phrases.english: Do we say: anything for הקדש, he fully decides and gives it over;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, כֹּל לְגַבֵּי נַפְשֵׁיהּ – לָא גָּמַר וּמַקְנֵי?
phrases.english: or maybe, anything that concerns himself, he does not fully decide to give it over?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling that taking back part of a gift cancels all of it, the גמרא opens a new set of questions about deathbed gifts made for holy purposes.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a שכיב מרע's הקדש of all his property stay in effect after he recovers?

steps.title: A dying man declared all his property ownerless
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks the same question about הפקר. Since anyone, poor or rich, may take הפקר, maybe it counts as a good deed he fully meant. Or maybe, since it is about his own life, he did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he made all his property ownerless, what is the law? Do we say that since it is open to the poor just as to the rich, he fully decides to give it up? Or maybe, when it is about himself, he does not fully decide?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a second, similar question, this time about a dying man who declared his property הפקר and then recovered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason to think הפקר might stand is that poor people can take from it, so it has a charity side to it. That might show he meant it fully. The other side is the same as before: his own survival is at stake, so maybe he did not mean it if he lived.

keyTerms.meaning: He declared it ownerless (הפקר), so anyone may take it
For the poor just like for the rich, since anyone can take it
Since, because

phrases.english: If he made all his property ownerless, what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן: כֵּיוָן דְּאַף לַעֲנִיִּים כַּעֲשִׁירִים –
phrases.english: Do we say: since it is open even to the poor, just as to the rich,
he fully decides and gives it over;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, כֹּל לְגַבֵּי נַפְשֵׁיהּ לָא גָּמַר וּמַקְנֵי?
phrases.english: or maybe, anything that concerns himself, he does not fully decide to give it over?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel question to step 19, applying the same doubt to הפקר instead of הקדש.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a שכיב מרע's הפקר of all his property stay in effect after he recovers?

steps.title: A dying man divided all his property among the poor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks the same question about צדקה. For charity he surely means it fully. Or maybe, since it is about his own life, he does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he divided all his property among the poor, what is the law? Do we say that with צדקה he certainly fully decides to give it over? Or maybe, when it is about himself, he does not fully decide?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a third, similar question about a dying man who gave everything to the poor as צדקה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This case has the strongest reason of the three to say the gift stands: giving straight to the poor is plain צדקה, so the first side of the question says he 'certainly' meant it fully. The other side brings back the same argument: since his own life was the reason for the gift, maybe he would not have given it all if he knew he would live.

keyTerms.meaning: He divided up and handed out
Charity to the poor
He certainly fully decides (doubled verb for emphasis)

phrases.english: If he divided all his property among the poor, what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמְרִינַן: צְדָקָה וַדַּאי מִגְמָר גָּמַר וּמַקְנֵי;
phrases.english: Do we say: with charity, he certainly fully decides and gives it over;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, כֹּל לְגַבֵּי נַפְשֵׁיהּ לָא גָּמַר וּמַקְנֵי?
phrases.english: or maybe, anything that concerns himself, he does not fully decide to give it over?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The third question in the series, applying the same doubt to giving charity to the poor.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a שכיב מרע's distribution of all his property to the poor stay in effect after he recovers?

steps.title: All three questions are left unanswered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends all three questions with תיקו: they stay unresolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand unanswered.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the three questions without deciding them. They are left as תיקו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source or argument is found to decide whether הקדש, הפקר or צדקה from a dying man stays in effect after he recovers. Both sides stay open: maybe a holy or charitable purpose shows he fully meant it, or maybe his own survival comes first.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question stays unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: A regular deathbed gift of everything is cancelled if the giver recovers. Whether this also applies to הקדש, הפקר or צדקה is left as תיקו.

phrases.english: Let it stand unresolved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the three questions of steps 19–21 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All three questions (הקדש, הפקר, צדקה by a dying man who recovered) stay unresolved.

steps.title: A second version of the same three questions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives another version of the questions in short form: הקדש, הפקר and dividing among the poor by a dying man. This version also ends in תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another version: if he made all his property holy, what is the law? If he made all his property ownerless, what is the law? If he divided all his property among the poor, what is the law? Let it stand unanswered.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of how the questions were asked. This version is shorter, with no reasons given for either side, and it also ends unresolved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same three cases are asked again, but this time without the words 'and recovered' and without the two sides of reasoning. The result is the same: none of the three questions is decided.

keyTerms.meaning: Another version, a different way the discussion was passed down
What is the law?

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new set of cases. It is the same three questions passed down in a different, shorter form.

phrases.english: Another version:
If he made all his property holy, what is the law?
If he made all his property ownerless, what is the law?
If he divided all his property among the poor, what is the law?
Let it stand unresolved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restates the three questions of steps 19–21 in a different, shorter version, also ending in תיקו.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the law when a שכיב מרע gives all his property to הקדש, declares it הפקר, or divides it among the poor?
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In this version too, all three questions remain unresolved.

steps.title: Four words that count as giving a gift
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת rules that 'shall take', 'shall gain possession', 'shall take hold' and 'shall acquire' are all words of giving a gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת says: if someone says 'So-and-so shall take', 'shall gain possession', 'shall take hold' or 'shall acquire' my property, all of these are words of a gift.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ruling from רב ששת about wording. He lists four words that each work to give property as a מתנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person giving away property does not have to say the exact word 'gift'. Any of these four words shows he wants the other person to own it. So each one is treated as a full gift.

keyTerms.meaning: He shall take
He shall gain possession
He shall take hold of it as owner
He shall acquire
Words that mean giving a gift

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet says:
'He shall take' and 'he shall gain possession'
and 'he shall take hold' and 'he shall acquire'
all of them are words of a gift.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the תיקו questions, the גמרא moves to a new topic: which words make a gift.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'יטול', 'יזכה', 'יחזיק' and 'יקנה' all work as words of a gift.

steps.title: A ברייתא adds two inheritance words
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that 'shall receive as inheritance' and 'shall inherit' also work, but only for someone fit to inherit him.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא taught: also 'he shall receive as inheritance' and 'he shall inherit' work, when said about someone who is fit to inherit him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that adds two more words to רב ששת's list. These two are inheritance words, not gift words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Inheritance words only make sense for a person who could inherit in the first place. So the ברייתא limits them to someone who is fit to inherit, like a son. For anyone else, these words would not work.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא
He shall receive as an inheritance
He shall inherit
Someone who is fit to inherit him

steps.confusionAlert: These two words do not work for just anyone. They work only for a person who could inherit him anyway.

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita:
also 'he shall receive as inheritance' and 'he shall inherit'
in the case of one fit to inherit him,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds two more words to רב ששת's list, with a limit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'יחסין' and 'ירת' work too, but only for someone fit to inherit.

steps.title: The ברייתא follows רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says this ברייתא follows the opinion of רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this ברייתא follows רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells us whose opinion the ברייתא follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא holds that a person may use inheritance words to leave his property to one who is fit to inherit him. The ברייתא's rule fits his view, so the גמרא links it to him.

phrases.english: and it is Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Identifies whose opinion the ברייתא in step 25 follows.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא about inheritance words follows רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא.
steps.whatToRemember: Gift words (יטול, יזכה, יחזיק, יקנה) work for anyone. Inheritance words (יחסין, ירת) work only for a fitting heir, following רבי יוחנן בן ברוקא.

steps.title: The גמרא opens a new set of questions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says a question was raised before the חכמים, setting up the next questions.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is about to bring a new set of questions, which come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: איבעיא להו only opens the question. The actual question comes in the next lines.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised before them (the חכמים)

phrases.english: A dilemma was raised before them:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new line of questions after the wording discussion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Not stated yet; the question itself follows.
